Every Friday at lunch, Dana sorted the lost-and-found bin outside the front office at Garfield Middle School. Nobody else had signed up for the job, and she had taken it mainly because it came with a pass out of the cafeteria.

Most of what turned up explained itself. A sweatshirt with a team name went to the coach. A math binder with a name on the cover went to that student's homeroom. Whatever was left at the end of the month went into a cardboard box for the clothing drive, and Mrs. Pell, the office secretary, kept the box ready under her desk.

The umbrella did not explain itself. It was black and enormous, the kind a doorman holds over a guest, and its wooden handle was carved into the head of a duck, worn smooth at the beak where a thumb had rested on it for years. It had been in the bin for three weeks.

"Somebody's grandfather," Mrs. Pell said when Dana held it up. "It goes in the box on the thirtieth. Nobody comes back for an umbrella, honey."

Dana leaned it against the wall and stood looking at it. A student would have been laughed out of the bus line for carrying a thing like that, and the teachers kept small folding umbrellas in their desks. So it belonged to someone who came into the building now and then but was not part of its daily life.

Visitors signed a sheet in a blue binder on the counter. Dana asked if she could look, and Mrs. Pell, already on the phone, waved a hand. On the Tuesday of the big storm three weeks back, the sheet held a dozen names: parents picking up sick children, a man delivering copier paper, and, at 2:40, a line in careful capital letters: T. MWANGI, CROSSING, PHONE.

Dana knew the crossing guard at the corner of Fifth and Garfield only as an orange vest and a raised hand. When the last bell rang it was drizzling, and she walked out to the corner with the umbrella under her arm. The guard stood in the wet with the vest's hood pulled up, waving a line of first graders across.

"Mr. Mwangi?" she said, and held it out handle first. He looked at the duck for a long moment before he took it. On the day of the storm, he told her, his radio had died, and he had gone into the office to call the district. He had stood the umbrella in the corner by the door, and when he came back for it after his shift, the office was locked. He had meant to ask about it, and then it had seemed too small a thing to trouble anyone with.

"It was my father's," he said, and opened it over the two of them.

On Monday, before the clothing-drive box could be taped shut, Dana pulled it out from under Mrs. Pell's desk and began going through it again, one sweater at a time, with the blue binder open beside her.

On the hill behind the water tower
my brother holds the spool in both fists
and asks me where the wind is.
I tell him to wait. You only see it

by what it borrows: the grass laid flat
in one long comb, a plastic bag
climbing the fence like a cat,
the flag at the school snapping its one word.

So we borrow it back. I walk the kite
downhill, thirty steps, and hold it up
by its two crossed sticks, and the string
goes tight between us like a held breath.

"Now," I say, and let go, and for a second
the kite only staggers, dips its nose,
considers the ground. Then something
takes it from underneath

and it goes up the way a hand goes up
in class when the answer is sure,
red diamond over the tower, its tail
writing the same quick letter over and over.

My brother leans back on his heels.
The spool jumps in his fists. He says
he can feel it, the whole sky pulling,
and asks if he is flying it or it is flying him.

I tell him that is the question. All afternoon
he lets out string and reels it in,
learning the pull the way you learn a dog
someone has handed you on a leash,

when to give and when to hold. By five
the gusts fall off. The kite comes down
in slow loops, like a leaf that has changed its mind,
and lands in the grass at our feet, light again,

just paper and two sticks and a tail of rags,
nothing you would look at twice.
My brother picks it up and turns it over,
looking, I think, for where the wind went in.

The summer I was eleven, I worked Saturdays at my aunt Lin's stall in the indoor market on Corbett Street. She sold vegetable seedlings in flats: tomatoes, peppers, basil, squash, each plant in its own plastic cell with a stick label in her small, square printing. My job was to water the flats at seven, make change, and wrap each sale in a sheet of newspaper so the soil stayed put on the bus ride home.

I was good at the selling part, or I thought I was. I had learned which plants looked best from the aisle and turned those flats to the front. When a customer hesitated, I told them how big the tomatoes would get. I had heard my aunt say it, so it seemed like a fact.

One Saturday in May a man in a paint-spattered jacket picked up a flat of six Brandywine tomatoes, the most expensive plants we had, and asked if they would do well along the north wall of his apartment building. I opened my mouth to say yes. My aunt spoke first. "They'll grow there," she said. "They won't give you a single tomato."

She asked him how many hours of sun the wall got. He thought about two, in the late afternoon. Tomatoes, she told him, wanted six or more. She walked him over to the lettuce, the mint, and the parsley, which could manage with less, and he left with a flat of lettuce that cost about a third of what the tomatoes would have.

I watched the money go. When he was out of earshot I said, as calmly as I could manage, that he had wanted the tomatoes and had been ready to pay for them, and that what happened on his wall afterward was his business. My aunt was wrapping a basil plant. A man who buys six tomato plants and gets no tomatoes, she said, comes back to the market one more time, to tell her about it, and after that he buys his plants at the hardware store.

I thought that was a long way around to explain losing money, and I said so. She handed me the basil to finish wrapping.

In late June the man in the paint-spattered jacket came back. He had a phone full of pictures of his lettuce, which had grown so well that he had been giving it away to the neighbors, and two of those neighbors had come with him. One of them had a balcony that faced south. My aunt sold her the six Brandywines.

I have worked in several stores since then, and more than once I have been trained to "overcome objections," which means to keep talking until a customer forgets the reason for hesitating. I always think of the north wall. My aunt did lose that first sale. She also knew something about the wall that the man was about to find out the slow way, and she counted that knowledge as part of what she was selling.

In 1831 the town of Hatherby, a cluster of farms and two mills on the Bessel River, built its first bridge. It was a plain timber span on stone piers, open to the sky, and for a few years the whole valley used it. By 1846 it was failing. Rain had soaked into the joints where the great beams met, and the wood there had gone soft enough to take a thumbnail. That spring two planks of the deck gave way under a hay wagon, and the town closed the bridge.

The man the selectmen hired to replace it, a millwright named Silas Dunmore, made a proposal that set the town talking. He would build the new bridge of timber, as before, but he would put a roof over it and board up its sides, so that the whole span looked like a long, narrow barn laid across the water. The roof and siding would add perhaps a fifth to the cost.

The town's treasurer, Ezra Coyle, spoke at the March meeting. Hatherby had borrowed to pay for the first bridge, he reminded the voters, and was still paying the debt. He asked what would happen if the roof cost more than Dunmore said, as such things usually did, and whether a town that could barely keep one bridge standing could afford to shingle one. Coyle sat down to murmurs. Then a farmer at the back asked whether Dunmore meant to keep cows in it, and the room laughed.

Dunmore answered with the old bridge itself. He had sawed a section from one of its beams, and he passed it around the room. The outside was gray and spongy; a few inches in, the wood was still sound. A timber bridge, he said, rotted at the joints, where water collected and stayed. The beams were the bridge. A deck could be replaced in a season, but the beams could not. Keep the rain off them, and they would last for generations.

The meeting voted for the roof by eleven votes, and the new bridge opened in the fall of 1848, painted red, with a small window cut in each side so that travelers could see the river.

It proved useful in ways no one at the March meeting had argued about. Travelers caught in storms waited inside it. Notices for auctions, lost horses, and church suppers were tacked to its inner walls until the boards were layered with paper. In winter the road crew had to shovel snow onto its floor, since the roof kept the deck bare and sleighs needed snow to slide on, and children were paid a penny a load to help.

Ezra Coyle crossed the bridge for the rest of his life, and in 1871, as an old man, he moved at a town meeting that Hatherby pay to reshingle its roof. The bridge carried traffic until 1934, when a steel bridge for automobiles was built downstream. By then it had stood eighty-six years, longer than any open bridge in the county had lasted.

Cut through the trunk of a pine or an oak and you will see a pattern of rings, light and dark, spreading out from the center like ripples from a dropped stone. Most people know that the rings can be counted to give a tree's age. Fewer know that the rings also hold a record of the weather the tree lived through, year by year, and that scientists have learned to read it.

The rings form because a tree in a climate with distinct seasons grows unevenly through the year. In spring, the thin layer of growing tissue just under the bark produces large, thin-walled cells, which look pale. As summer goes on, the new cells become smaller and denser, and the wood they make looks darker. Growth stops in winter, so the next spring's pale wood begins sharply against the last summer's dark wood. One light band and one dark band together make a single year's ring.

The width of each ring depends on how well the tree grew that year, and that depends heavily on conditions. In dry regions water is often the limit, so a wet year tends to leave a wide ring and a drought year a narrow one. In cold places, such as high on a mountain, summer warmth may matter more. A scientist who studies tree rings therefore reads a ring's width as a clue to the climate, though never a perfect one, since a fire, an insect outbreak, or a crowding neighbor can also slow a tree's growth.

Single trees can mislead, which is why the method depends on matching. Trees in the same region live through the same dry and wet years, so they tend to share the same sequence of narrow and wide rings. By lining up the pattern from a living tree with the pattern in an older dead one, and that one with a still older beam from a building, researchers can link samples into a chain that runs far past the life of any one tree. This matching, called cross-dating, also catches errors: in a very hard year some trees form almost no ring, and in an unusual year a tree may form two.

The study began in the early 1900s with an American astronomer, A. E. Douglass, who hoped tree rings might show a link between sunspots and the weather. That link remained uncertain, but his method spread. Today, sequences built this way reach back more than ten thousand years in parts of Europe, and in the American Southwest, ring patterns in old roof beams have been used to date when pueblo villages were built.

Researchers today rarely need to cut a tree down. They use a hollow drill about as thick as a pencil to pull out a thin core from bark to center, and the small hole it leaves usually does the tree little harm. Some of the longest records come from bristlecone pines in the mountains of California and Nevada, a few of which have been growing for more than four thousand years.
